text:
As part of its commitment to sustainability and reducing carbon emissions, Vancouver International Airport (YVR) has launched a new tool for passengers to be part of the transition to a lower-carbon aviation industry.

YVR’s online calculator allows travellers to estimate their flight’s greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and contribute to the use of Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF).

Contributions made through YVR’s new online calculator will be applied to environmental attributes associated with SAF and will enable airlines’ further use of SAF, starting with Air Canada.

SAF’s environmental attributes are the quantified climate benefits or reductions associated with its use, such as the GHG emissions avoided by not extracting non-renewable resources used for fossil jet fuel. Contributing to these attributes supports SAF growth and is essential for scaling SAF globally, as it bolsters activity across the supply chain.

“Sustainable Aviation Fuel is one of the most effective options available today to make meaningful progress towards decarbonizing aviation. This new tool gives travellers the opportunity to help increase the use of SAF and support more sustainable air travel,” said Tamara Vrooman, president and CEO at Vancouver International Airport.

SAF is a lower-carbon alternative to fossil jet fuel. It is made from renewable and waste-derived materials and, depending on the feedstock, production pathway and lifecycle-assessment methodology, can have lower lifecycle GHG emissions than fossil jet fuel.

Certain SAF may achieve lifecycle GHG reductions of up to 80 percent when used in neat form compared with fossil jet fuel. As a “drop-in” fuel, it can be blended with fossil jet fuel and requires no changes to today’s aircraft or existing airport infrastructure.

While SAF is currently in use by some airlines, including those operating at YVR, as an emerging fuel source, limited production and higher prices are obstacles for wider uptake. As production increases and more supply becomes available, costs are likely to lower, increasing the proportion of SAF to be likely used in flights around the world.

This initiative is part of YVR’s broader efforts to raise awareness of SAF and support airline partners in increasing their SAF use to advance the aviation industry’s goal of net zero emissions by 2050.

While voluntary contributions through YVR’s online calculator help support the broader adoption of SAF by Air Canada over time, the tool is available to all passengers regardless of which airline they travel on.

Every flight is a chance to make a difference. Calculate the GHG emissions for your next flight and contribute to supporting SAF: Support sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) on your next flight.

text:
SkyNRG and KLM have started the construction of DSL-01, the Netherlands’ first facility fully dedicated to the production of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF).

Located in Delfzijl, the project marks a major milestone in scaling up SAF production in the Netherlands and advancing the decarbonisation of aviation.

Developed by SkyNRG, DSL-01 is also the first commercial-scale SAF plant globally to secure non-recourse project financing, highlighting growing confidence in scalable SAF production and establishing a model for future sustainable fuel projects worldwide.

KLM Dutch Royal Airlines is the primary off-taker for the SAF produced, playing a key role in enabling the project through its long-term offtake commitment.

Once fully operational in 2028, the facility is expected to produce approximately 100,000 tonnes of SAF annually using low-quality feedstocks such as used cooking oil and residual fats and greases.

Through the Hydroprocessed Esters and Fatty Acids (HEFA) pathway, the facility will produce SAF with significantly lower lifecycle emissions compared to conventional jet fuel, while also generating renewable co-products including propane, butane, and naphtha.

Marjan Rintel, CEO KLM, said: “As the world’s first airline, our long-term offtake guarantee directly contributes to the financing and realisation of this facility. And today, this project finally becomes tangible as we celebrate the groundbreaking together with SkyNRG and other guests. I’m proud that KLM, as a founding member of SkyNRG and its largest DSL-01’s fuel customer, is taking an important step in scaling up SAF production in the Netherlands and advancing the sustainability of aviation.”

Maarten van Dijk, CEO SkyNRG, added:“The start of construction of DSL-01 marks a defining moment for sustainable aviation. This project demonstrates that large scale SAF production is moving from ambition to implementation. Together with committed partners like KLM, we are building critical infrastructure that will help accelerate aviation transition towards lower emissions while strengthening Europe’s sustainable fuel industry. The project will also create more than 100 direct jobs, further reinforcing the northern Netherlands as a leading hub for industry innovation and energy transition.”

text:
Renewable fuels company EcoCeres has partnered with SF Group and China National Aviation Fuel Group (CNAF) to supply blended sustainable aviation fuel for outbound freighter flights operated by SF Airlines. The programme, in which SAF produced by EcoCeres will be blended by CNAF, involves collaboration with the Second Research Institute of the Civil Aviation Administration of China (CASRI). The SAF will be supplied to SF Airlines’ cargo hub at Ezhou Huahu International Airport in Hubei, which is considered a key aviation gateway under China’s 14th Five-Year Plan for Port Development. Elsewhere in Asia, Malaysia-based FatHopes Energy has entered a strategic partnership with PetroVietnam Oil Corporation (PVOIL) to establish Vietnam’s first nationwide used cooking oil collection ecosystem that is expected to aggregate more than 200,000 tonnes of feedstock annually for SAF production.

The EcoCeres project follows a prior SAF pilot programme in China, called Project Spark, in which SAF produced at EcoCeres’ Zhangjiagang facility was blended by CNAF and used to fuel commercial flights at Chengdu Shuangliu International Airport, that validated the full value chain from production and transportation to blending and deployment.

The new project with SF Airlines also includes application of Anchor Trace, a platform developed by CNAF and CASRI to transfer Scope 1 emissions to airlines and Scope 3 emissions to corporate customers. It enables full lifecycle tracking, registration and retirement of SAF environmental attributes.

By integrating renewable fuel production, a transparent environmental attribute tracking system and real-world aviation logistics demand, the project validates a decarbonisation model that is both technically viable and commercially sustainable, says EcoCeres.

“This project demonstrates how SAF can pragmatically and efficiently connect renewable fuel producers, aviation fuel infrastructure providers and cargo operators in a results-oriented way,” said James Tam, Co-Chairman of the Hong Kong-based company. “By integrating SAF into existing aviation fuel systems, we are working together with our partners to build a replicable, scalable and verifiable pathway for lower emissions air cargo development in China.”

Headquartered in Shenzhen, Guangdong, SF Airlines operates around 90 freighters through four major aviation hubs: Shenzhen, Hangzhou, Beijing and Ezhou.

“The successful inaugural flight of this project marks SF Group’s enhanced end-to-end capability, from bulk SAF sourcing, blending and customised fuelling to freighter utilisation, alongside a strategic green capacity deployment,” commented Li Sheng, Chairman of SF Airlines. “It also positions SF Airlines as the first in China to integrate three unique advantages: a SAF-enabled hub airport, large-scale physical SAF fuelling capability and international SAF certification, thus making it a Scope 3 green aviation service provider.”

EcoCeres’ SAF is produced from waste and residue feedstocks via its proprietary process, which it says delivers up to 90% lifecycle greenhouse gas emission reductions compared to conventional jet fuel.

Meanwhile, FatHopes Energy and PVOIL are to establish an integrated ecosystem capable of collecting, tracing and managing used cooking oil (UCO) across Vietnam for use as SAF feedstock, commencing with an initial rollout in Ho Chi Minh City before expanding across the country.

FatHopes proprietary waste recycling management system is a digital platform that provides end-to-end traceability throughout the collection journey, ensuring compliance, says the company, with international sustainability requirements and meeting global certification standards.

PVOIL and its dedicated collection subsidiary, PVOIL Trans, will lead the implementation and expansion of the initiative throughout Vietnam, engaging with businesses, communities and local stakeholders to establish what it expects to be one of the country’s most comprehensive waste-to-energy collection networks.

“By leveraging our nationwide network together with FatHopes Energy’s innovative technology and international expertise, we are creating a modern and transparent collection ecosystem that not only delivers environmental benefits but also contributes to the future development of sustainable aviation fuel in Vietnam,” said Mai Trung Thanh, Director of PVOIL Trans.

The aggregation of an anticipated 200,000 tonnes of feedstock annually will be exported to support FatHopes Energy’s proposed biorefinery in Malaysia that is intended to serve as a regional hub for processing waste feedstocks into SAF.

“By combining FatHopes Energy’s expertise in digital traceability, feedstock collection and sustainable aviation fuel supply chains with PVOIL’s nationwide reach and operational capabilities, we are building the infrastructure needed to support Vietnam’s energy transition while strengthening Southeast Asia’s role in the global sustainable aviation ecosystem,” said Vinesh Sinha, the company’s CEO. “We believe this partnership will serve as a blueprint for how countries across the region can unlock the value of waste, accelerate decarbonisation and create long-term environmental and economic impact.”

text:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty and Qatari Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani praised the notable progress in Egyptian-Qatari relations under the directives of the two countries' leaderships, highlighting the growing pace of high-level visits and continued coordination and consultations on various regional issues.

The remarks came during a meeting between Abdelatty and Sheikh Mohammed on Thursday, August 20, 2026, ahead of the seventh session of the Egyptian-Qatari Joint Higher Committee, being held in the city of El Alamein.

The two sides affirmed their shared commitment to further developing bilateral relations across various fields.

They also stressed the need for the Joint Higher Committee to convene regularly on an annual basis, emphasizing the importance of building on the outcomes of its seventh session and translating them into practical steps, while continuing to update the contractual framework governing bilateral relations.

The two sides welcomed the notable development in economic and investment relations. Abdelatty noted that trade between Egypt and Qatar increased by 80 percent in 2025, highlighting the significant growth in investment cooperation, particularly following the announcement of the Ras El Hekma deal in November 2025 and the launch by Qatari Diar of work on the project's first phase on August 9.

He also pointed to the launch of a sustainable aviation fuel manufacturing project in the Suez Canal Economic Zone with direct Qatari investments, describing it as a reflection of confidence in Egypt's investment climate and the promising opportunities offered by the Egyptian economy.

On consular cooperation, Abdelatty praised the care extended to the Egyptian community in Qatar, stressing the importance of convening the joint labor committee at the earliest opportunity. He affirmed Egypt's readiness to provide the professional cadres and specialists needed by the Qatari labor market through the electronic labor-matching system and the Overseas Employment Management Unit, ensuring an organized movement of workers that serves the interests of both countries.

The two sides also discussed regional developments and efforts to de-escalate tensions and contain instability in the region. They stressed the importance of prioritizing political and diplomatic solutions and returning to the memorandum of understanding between the United States and Iran and building on it to resume the negotiating track, with a view to reaching a final and lasting agreement that addresses the concerns of all parties and contributes to regional security and stability.

They also underscored the importance of ensuring the security, safety and freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz in accordance with international law, and refraining from any measures that could impede international navigation and trade, given their direct implications for energy security, supply chains and the global economy.

The two sides exchanged views on developments in the Palestinian issue, stressing the importance of continued close coordination with the United States and regional partners to ensure implementation of the US president's peace plan for the Gaza Strip and to press Israel to fulfill its commitments under the first phase and the announced roadmap.

They also discussed the serious developments in the West Bank and Jerusalem, warning against settlement expansion, escalating settler attacks, incursions and provocations at Al-Aqsa Mosque. They stressed the need to halt unilateral Israeli measures, given their serious repercussions for prospects for peace and stability and for the situation across the region.

Regarding Lebanon, the two sides stressed the importance of continued Egyptian-Qatari coordination in support of Lebanon's security, stability, sovereignty and territorial integrity, as well as the need for Israel's complete withdrawal from Lebanese territory and support for the country's national institutions, foremost among them the Lebanese Army.

They also discussed developments in Sudan, warning of the deteriorating humanitarian situation and reaffirming their support for Sudan's unity, sovereignty, territorial integrity and national institutions, while rejecting any attempts to partition the country or establish parallel entities.

The meeting also addressed developments in the Horn of Africa. The two sides stressed the need to respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the countries of the region and refrain from any unilateral moves that threaten regional peace and security or seek to impose access to maritime routes by force in violation of international law.

Abdelatty, for his part, reviewed Egypt's participation in the second summit of troop-contributing countries to the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM), held in Kampala late last July. He stressed the importance of providing the mission with the necessary funding and support and preserving the security and stability gains achieved in Somalia over the past years, in a manner that safeguards the interests of countries in the region and prevents the resurgence of terrorist threats.

The two sides agreed to maintain close coordination and consultations between Egypt and Qatar and build on the momentum in bilateral relations and the outcomes of the seventh session of the Joint Higher Committee, with a view to advancing ties to broader horizons and strengthening their ability to address shared regional challenges.

Abstract

Sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) deployment requires simultaneous coordination of spatially distributed biomass supply chains and nonlinear conversion technologies. This study develops an integrated multiscale optimization framework for SAF production in Mexico using second-generation sugarcane bagasse as the lignocellulosic resource for alcohol-intermediate production, followed by an intensified Alcohol-to-Jet (ATJ) upgrading stage targeting Mexico City Airport. A multi-period mixed-integer linear programming model optimizes harvest-area selection, biorefinery location, biomass allocation, inventory, production, and distribution, while an Aspen Plus model of an intensified Alcohol-to-Jet (ATJ) process with reactive distillation is optimized using Differential Evolution with Tabu List. In this framework, the ATJ block is not modeled as direct biomass-to-jet conversion. In the base case, ethanol is used as the representative alcohol intermediate. Therefore, the upstream biomass-to-alcohol section is represented through an effective bagasse-to-ethanol coefficient, whereas the Aspen Plus–DETL model explicitly describes the downstream ethanol-to-ATJ-range hydrocarbon blendstock upgrading section through dehydration, ethylene oligomerization, hydrogenation, and fractionation. Process yield, production cost, environmental impact, and feasible capacity are fed back into the supply chain model, making process performance endogenous rather than fixed. Results show that the decoupled supply chain baseline favors large production capacities, reducing TAC from approximately 1010 to 340 USD/tSAF and system-level EI99 from 1.110 to 1.059 kPt EI99/tSAF as capacity increases from 80,000 to 490,000 tSAF/year. This corresponds to an environmental reduction of approximately 5.2%. In contrast, isolated ATJ optimization exhibits nonlinear scale-dependent behavior, with process-only EI99 decreasing from approximately 1.70 to 0.55 kPt EI99/tSAF. The integrated framework identifies an intermediate capacity region of 120,000–300,000 tSAF/year, with TAC values of approximately 3400–6800 USD/tSAF and total EI99 values of approximately 0.78–1.31 kPt EI99/tSAF. The integrated base case at 200,000 tSAF/year has an EI99 value of approximately 1.063 kPt EI99/tSAF.

1. Introduction

The aviation sector is one of the most difficult transport sectors to decarbonize because it depends on high-energy-density liquid fuels and long-lived aircraft and infrastructure. According to the International Energy Agency, aviation accounts for approximately 2–3% of global energy-related CO2 emissions and close to 12% of transport-related emissions, with emissions rebounding to nearly 950 Mt CO2 in recent years as air traffic recovered. Demand for air travel could more than double by 2050, which increases the need for mitigation options that can be implemented without replacing the existing aviation system. Sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) is therefore considered a key near-term option because it can be used as a drop-in fuel in current aircraft and fuel distribution infrastructure. However, large-scale SAF deployment depends not only on conversion technology, but also on feedstock availability, logistics, production cost, environmental performance and regional demand [1,2].

SAF production can be developed through different certified and emerging pathways, each one with specific feedstock requirements, process constraints and supply chain implications. Among them, the Alcohol-to-Jet (ATJ) pathway has received considerable attention because alcohol intermediates can be upgraded into jet-range hydrocarbons through dehydration, oligomerization, hydrogenation and final fractionation [3,4]. ATJ-SPK is recognized under ASTM D7566 as an alcohol-derived synthetic paraffinic kerosene blendstock, with eligible alcohol-related feedstocks including ethanol, isobutanol and isobutene from biomass, and a typical maximum blend ratio of 50% with conventional jet fuel [5]. In biomass-based ATJ systems, however, the lignocellulosic resource is not converted directly into aviation hydrocarbons. Biomass-derived carbohydrates must first be converted into an alcohol intermediate, which is then upgraded through the ATJ process. This distinction is important for process and supply chain modeling because biomass availability, alcohol yield, hydrogen demand and upgrading performance affect different parts of the production system.

From a supply chain perspective, SAF production involves geographically dispersed biomass resources, seasonal availability, storage requirements, transport decisions and capital-intensive conversion facilities. mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) models have been widely used to optimize this type of system because they can represent facility location, biomass allocation, inventory management, production planning and product distribution. García and You [2] showed that supply chain design is a major driver of competitiveness in biomass-based process systems. Similarly, Galanopoulos et al. [6] showed that network design decisions can significantly affect the techno-economic performance of biorefineries. Nonetheless, many supply chain models represent the conversion process using fixed coefficients for yield, energy consumption, operating cost and environmental burden. This simplification is practical, but it can affect strategic conclusions when process performance changes with scale or operating conditions. Recent supply chain studies have also emphasized the role of metaheuristic algorithms for large-scale or computationally challenging network design problems. For example, Akbari-Aghghaleh et al. [7] developed a mixed-integer linear programming framework for a perishable closed-loop poultry supply chain and evaluated Differential Evolution, Simulated Annealing, Genetic Algorithm, and hybrid metaheuristic variants for different problem sizes. Their results highlight the usefulness of metaheuristic methods when exact solution of large supply chain models becomes computationally demanding. Similar trends have been reported in sustainable and closed-loop supply chain network design, where metaheuristics are frequently used to handle large-scale, multi-period, multi-echelon, or uncertainty-aware formulations [8].

In the present work, the supply chain layer is solved as a MILP using CPLEX because the case study scale remains tractable and the exact solver provides a controlled optimality gap for the network decisions. Metaheuristic optimization is used at the process level through the DETL algorithm, where the Aspen Plus model introduces nonlinear, simulation-based, and potentially nonconvex behavior. Therefore, the contribution of this work is not to replace the MILP solver with a metaheuristic, but to integrate exact supply chain optimization with metaheuristic process-level optimization in a sequential MILP–Aspen Plus–DETL framework.

Process performance in biofuel systems is sensitive to design choices, thermodynamic constraints, separation efficiency, heat integration and hydrogen consumption. Grossmann [9] showed that decoupling process and supply chain decisions can lead to suboptimal enterprise-wide solutions because interactions between decision levels are neglected. In SAF systems, this issue is particularly relevant because plant location and capacity are linked to feedstock logistics, while process configuration affects cost, environmental impact and feasible production scale. Consequently, a supply chain model based on fixed process parameters may identify a network that appears optimal under assumed coefficients, but does not reflect the behavior of the actual conversion system.

At the process level, detailed simulations have been used to evaluate ATJ performance with greater rigor. Aspen Plus models can describe thermodynamic behavior, reaction–separation interactions and techno-economic indicators for alternative configurations. Romero-Izquierdo et al. [10] showed that process intensification can reduce energy consumption and total annualized cost in ATJ systems. More recently, Contreras-Zarazúa et al. [11] and Huerta-Rosas et al. [12] demonstrated that reactive distillation can improve economic and environmental performance by integrating reaction and separation. These studies confirm the importance of process design for SAF viability. However, they are usually carried out at plant scale under fixed feed and production conditions, without considering how regional biomass logistics, plant capacity and airport demand can modify the preferred operating region.

Several studies have attempted to connect supply chain optimization with process simulation. Galanopoulos et al. [6] proposed an iterative framework linking MILP models with Aspen-based simulations for biorefinery techno-economic assessment. Panteli et al. [13] developed a superstructure-based MILP model that incorporates multiple processing technologies into supply chain design. These approaches represent important advances, but they often rely on simplified process representations or surrogate models to keep the optimization tractable. Moreover, they are not focused on SAF-specific ATJ systems with intensified process configurations. In Mexico, Matos-Ríos et al. [14] showed that optimal renewable aviation fuel supply chains depend strongly on regional biomass availability and logistics. As in many supply chain studies, however, process performance was treated as an external input. Therefore, the main goal of this work is to develop an integrated multiscale optimization framework for SAF production in Mexico by coupling a strategic MILP supply chain model with a rigorous Aspen Plus simulation of an intensified ATJ upgrading process. The process design and operating conditions are optimized using Differential Evolution with Tabu List (DETL), allowing nonlinear and nonconvex process behavior to be explored. The framework is applied to the production of ATJ-range hydrocarbon blendstock from a sugarcane bagasse-derived ethanol intermediate, with Mexico City Airport as the primary demand node. In this formulation, sugarcane bagasse is treated as the upstream lignocellulosic resource for alcohol-intermediate production, while the intensified ATJ model represents the downstream alcohol-to-ATJ-range hydrocarbon blendstock upgrading step.

The proposed framework updates process yield, production cost, environmental burden, hydrogen demand, utility consumption and feasible capacity within the supply chain model instead of imposing them as fixed parameters. The model simultaneously optimizes biorefinery location, biomass allocation and production planning, while environmental performance is evaluated using the Eco-indicator 99 methodology [15]. This structure avoids collapsing the complete bagasse-to-SAF pathway into a single direct conversion coefficient and allows the effect of process-level behavior on network-level decisions to be evaluated explicitly.

The main contribution of this work is threefold. First, it introduces an iterative MILP–Aspen Plus–DETL framework in which intensified ATJ process performance is updated endogenously within a regional SAF supply chain model. Second, it separates the upstream biomass-to-alcohol conversion from the downstream alcohol-to-ATJ-range hydrocarbon blendstock upgrading step, which improves the interpretation of feedstock, process, and supply chain assumptions. Third, it evaluates whether decoupled and integrated optimization lead to different conclusions regarding plant capacity, cost and environmental performance. Price volatility, policy incentives and stochastic uncertainty are not included in the base case, but the proposed framework provides a structured basis for incorporating process-level realism into regional SAF deployment planning. The remainder of this paper presents the supply chain and process models, the coupling strategy, the computational implementation, and the economic and environmental results.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1. System Boundary and ATJ Pathway Definition

Figure 1 shows the system boundary adopted in this work. The pathway is divided into two sections: an upstream biomass-to-alcohol section and a downstream Alcohol-to-Jet (ATJ) upgrading section. Sugarcane bagasse is used as the lignocellulosic resource because of its availability in Mexico and its relevance as a non-edible agricultural residue [16,17]. The ATJ process does not use raw lignocellulosic biomass as the direct feed to jet-range hydrocarbons. Instead, bagasse-derived carbohydrates are first converted into an alcohol intermediate, which is then upgraded through dehydration, oligomerization, hydrogenation, and fractionation [3,4,18].

The upstream section includes bagasse collection, pretreatment, enzymatic hydrolysis, fermentation, and alcohol separation. These stages provide the alcohol intermediate required by the ATJ section. In the base case, ethanol is used as the representative alcohol intermediate. This upstream biomass-to-ethanol section is not simulated in Aspen Plus. It is represented in the supply chain model through an effective sugarcane bagasse-to-ethanol coefficient, β E t O H , which includes pretreatment, hydrolysis, fermentation, ethanol recovery, and associated material losses. In the revised base case, βEtOH is interpreted as an effective recovered-ethanol coefficient that includes both C6 and C5 sugar contributions from dry sugarcane bagasse. The coefficient therefore accounts for cellulose-derived glucose fermentation and hemicellulose-derived C5 sugar co-fermentation, together with ethanol recovery/purification losses. This coefficient is not a direct bagasse-to-SAF yield and remains separate from the downstream ethanol-to-ATJ-range hydrocarbon blendstock upgrading yield calculated by the Aspen Plus–DETL model.

The downstream section starts from the ethanol intermediate. This part is explicitly simulated in Aspen Plus and optimized through the DETL algorithm. The modeled sequence includes ethanol dehydration to ethylene, olefin oligomerization in an intensified reactive distillation configuration, hydrogenation, and final fractionation into ATJ-range hydrocarbon blendstock cut and co-product streams. The Aspen Plus–DETL block returns the process yield, specific production cost, environmental burden, hydrogen demand, utility consumption, and feasible capacity bounds used by the supply chain model.

At the supply chain level, the MILP model represents biomass availability, harvest-area selection, biomass transport, storage, candidate biorefinery location, ethanol-intermediate production requirements, ATJ-range hydrocarbon blendstock production, inventory, and delivery to the airport demand node. The upstream coefficient β E t O H links bagasse input with ethanol-intermediate availability, whereas the Aspen Plus–DETL results describe the downstream ethanol-to-ATJ-range hydrocarbon blendstock upgrading performance. This structure keeps the biochemical conversion and the ATJ upgrading step separate, avoiding the use of a single direct bagasse-to-SAF conversion coefficient.

The product from the downstream ATJ block is reported as ATJ-range hydrocarbon blendstock before final blending. ASTM D7566 Annex A5 defines the technical ATJ-SPK pathway for alcohol-derived synthetic paraffinic kerosene and its blending limit with conventional Jet A/A-1 [5]. This recognition is used here only to define the fuel pathway and product interpretation. CORSIA eligibility, emission-reduction claims, and final fuel certification require separate life cycle greenhouse gas assessment and fuel property testing [19,20]. Therefore, this study reports ATJ-range hydrocarbon blendstock production and uses Eco-indicator 99 as an environmental screening metric, but it does not claim CORSIA certification or final ASTM qualification of the modeled fuel.

2.2. Integrated Problem Statement

The proposed framework is formulated as an integrated multiscale optimization problem that couples supply chain decisions with process-design and operating decisions. This formulation follows the enterprise-wide optimization perspective, where supply, production, conversion, and distribution decisions are coordinated within the same decision structure, rather than solved as independent problems [9]. For SAF systems, this coordination is relevant because biomass availability, seasonal logistics, plant capacity, hydrogen demand, utility consumption, and process performance jointly affect deployment cost and feasibility [2,14,21].

The framework contains two main blocks. The first block is a multi-period supply chain MILP model that determines harvest-area selection, biomass transport, biomass inventory, biorefinery location, production scheduling, ATJ-range hydrocarbon blendstock inventory, and distribution to the airport demand node. The second block is an Aspen Plus–DETL process model that evaluates the intensified ATJ upgrading section under the feed and production conditions imposed by the supply chain solution. The purpose of the coupling is to update process performance inside the network model instead of using fixed yield, cost, environmental, hydrogen, utility, and capacity coefficients.

Let x denote the vector of supply chain decision variables, including harvest-area selection, biomass flows, biomass inventory, biorefinery location, production scheduling, product inventory, and airport distribution. Let z denote the vector of process-design and operating variables of the intensified ATJ process, including reactive distillation design variables, operating conditions, hydrogen consumption, utility demand, and fractionation performance. The integrated optimization problem is expressed in compact form as follows:

min x , z T A C x , z , E I x , z

(2)

(3)

where T A C ( x , z ) is the total annualized cost of the integrated SAF system, and E I ( x , z ) is the environmental impact expressed in Eco-indicator 99 kpoints. The function g S C represents the supply chain constraints, including biomass availability, storage, location, production, inventory, and distribution constraints. The function g P represents the process-level feasibility constraints evaluated by the Aspen Plus–DETL block. The term h C represents the coupling relationships between the network and process levels.

The vector θ ( z ) contains the process-derived coefficients returned by the Aspen Plus–DETL block to the MILP. These coefficients include ATJ upgrading yield, specific process cost, specific environmental burden, hydrogen demand, utility intensity, and feasible capacity bounds. The vector ψ ( x ) contains the network-derived boundary conditions sent from the MILP to the process model, mainly the production target, ethanol-intermediate feed rate, and operating window.

Two configurations are evaluated. In the decoupled baseline, conversion yield, specific production cost, environmental burden, hydrogen demand, utility consumption, and feasible capacity are fixed inputs in the supply chain model. In the integrated configuration, these quantities are recalculated by the Aspen Plus–DETL block and returned to the MILP during the outer-loop iterations. Thus, the network solution is obtained using process coefficients that depend on the selected production scale and operating conditions.

Figure 2 summarizes the iterative MILP–Aspen Plus–DETL coupling strategy. At each iteration, the supply chain MILP sends the production target, ethanol-intermediate feed rate, and operating window to the Aspen Plus–DETL process block. The process block then returns updated ATJ yield, specific cost, environmental burden, hydrogen demand, utility intensity, and feasible capacity bounds. This exchange is repeated until the convergence criterion is satisfied.

2.3. Supply Chain MILP Formulation

The supply chain model is formulated as a deterministic, multi-period mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) problem. The network includes biomass harvest centers, candidate biorefinery locations, and Mexico City Airport as the demand node. The geographic distribution of biomass availability, harvest centers, candidate biorefinery locations, and the airport node is provided in Figure S1 and Tables S1–S3 of the Supplementary Materials. Available quantities of sugarcane bagasse and corn stover were sourced from SIAP [22], while the specific fuel demand data for the airport node were obtained from ASA [23]. Geographic coordinates were transformed into planar (X)–(Y) coordinates, expressed in kilometers relative to a common reference origin, to calculate transport distances consistently across the network. A monthly planning horizon is used to represent seasonal biomass availability, biomass degradation, inventory dynamics, production scheduling, and product distribution. This structure is commonly used in biomass and biofuel supply chain design because it allows facility location, capacity activation, transport flows, production planning, and storage decisions to be optimized simultaneously [2,14].

The economic objective minimizes the total annualized cost of the supply chain system:

min T A C = C b a g r a w + C u p + C t r , b i o + C i n v , b i o + C c a p + C A T J d i r + C H 2 + u t i l + C i n v , S A F + C T R , s a f

The direct ATJ term excludes purchased hydrogen and utilities, whereas the annualized capacity term excludes the downstream ATJ equipment contribution. Detailed numerical definitions and the complete TAC are provided in Section S8 of the Supplementary Materials. For interpretation purposes, the Total Annual Cost (TAC) objective was also disaggregated into its main cost components: biomass acquisition, biomass transportation, biomass inventory/storage, annualized biorefinery capacity, Aspen Plus–DETL process contribution, hydrogen and utility contributions, ATJ-range hydrocarbon blendstock inventory, and final product transportation. This decomposition was not introduced as an additional objective function; it was used only to interpret the difference between the decoupled and integrated scenarios. 2.4. Intensified ATJ Process Simulation and Optimization Variables

The Aspen Plus model represents the downstream ethanol-to-ATJ-range hydrocarbon blendstock upgrading section. The feed to this block is ethanol obtained from the upstream biomass-to-alcohol section defined in Section 2.1. Raw sugarcane bagasse is not introduced into the Aspen Plus process model.

The simulated ATJ route includes four main stages. First, ethanol is dehydrated to ethylene. Second, ethylene is converted into higher olefinic intermediates through oligomerization. Third, the olefinic products are hydrogenated to paraffinic hydrocarbons. Finally, the hydrocarbon mixture is fractionated into an ATJ-range hydrocarbon blendstock cut and heavier co-product streams. This sequence follows the core ATJ pathway for upgrading alcohols into jet-range hydrocarbon blendstocks [3,4].

Process intensification is introduced in the oligomerization–separation section. In this configuration, reaction and separation are integrated through a reactive distillation-based system, following the principle that combined reaction–separation units can reduce equipment count, improve energy efficiency, and modify equilibrium-limited behavior [11,12,27]. The reactive distillation configuration used for the ethylene-to-SAF upgrading step is shown in Figure S3 of the Supplementary Materials.

A literature-normalized ATJ/ETJ benchmark was incorporated to contextualize the process-level contribution of the reactive distillation-based configuration. The benchmark considers four reference levels: Rivas-Interian et al. [18] as the closest distributed biomass–ethanol–biojet process for Mexico, the ATJ/ETJ review by Wang and Tao [3] as the conventional pathway reference, and the intensified ATJ studies of Villareal-Hernández et al. [28] and Contreras-Zarazúa et al. [11] as process-intensification references.

This benchmark was not introduced as an additional supply chain scenario and was not intended to replace a full Aspen Plus simulation of a conventional ATJ process. Rather, it provides a process-level reference for interpreting the intensified oligomerization–separation configuration under a common ethanol-intermediate and ATJ-range hydrocarbon blendstock product interpretation. The decoupled and integrated MILP scenarios were then used to evaluate the separate system-level effect of propagating process-performance coefficients into regional supply chain decisions. Details of the benchmark and normalization basis are provided in Section S5 of the Supplementary Materials.

The reactive distillation column was represented in Aspen Plus using equilibrium stages for vapor–liquid phase calculations. Chemical reactions assigned to the designated reactive stages were evaluated using the literature-based kinetic expressions adopted from Villareal-Hernández et al. [28] for ethylene oligomerization and olefin hydrogenation. Therefore, the term “equilibrium” refers exclusively to the vapor–liquid equilibrium formulation of the column stages and does not imply chemical equilibrium or Gibbs equilibrium reaction modeling.

The overall stoichiometric relationships for ethanol dehydration, ethylene oligomerization, and olefin hydrogenation were used to define the reaction sequence and to verify carbon and hydrogen balances. They were not used as substitutes for the kinetic rate expressions in the reactive stages. Catalyst deactivation, aging, regeneration, and long-term selectivity decay were not included. Consequently, the model is used as a steady-state process-performance generator, rather than as a predictive model of catalyst lifetime.

Catalyst behavior was therefore represented through the kinetic reaction network, operating conditions, conversion/selectivity behavior, and reactive distillation feasibility constraints reported for the intensified ATJ process. Catalyst deactivation, time-dependent activity loss, catalyst regeneration, and long-term selectivity decay were not included. This modeling choice is consistent with the objective of the present work, which is to generate process-performance coefficients for integration with the MILP supply chain model, rather than to perform catalyst lifetime prediction.

The Aspen Plus–DETL model was validated at the process-performance level using simulation convergence, carbon balance closure, hydrogen consumption consistency, carbon number distribution, SAF-range product definition, utility demand, and comparison with literature-reported ATJ and intensified ATJ systems. The kinetic source, modeling assumptions, and validation criteria are summarized in Section S4 of the Supplementary Materials.

The modeled product stream was defined as the liquid fraction enriched in C8–C16 hydrocarbons. Based on the simulated component distribution, the cut contains approximately 81.10 wt% paraffinic hydrocarbons and 18.90 wt% residual α-olefins. It is therefore reported as a C8–C16 ATJ-range hydrocarbon blendstock, rather than as ATJ-SPK-equivalent material. The product label is a process model classification used for yield, cost, and supply chain calculations. Complete olefin saturation, fuel property testing, ASTM D7566 qualification, and blending evaluation are outside the scope of the present model. [5].
