Eco-indicator 99 (EI99) was used as the environmental metric because the integrated optimization framework requires a single scalar environmental coefficient that can be exchanged between the Aspen Plus–DETL process block and the MILP supply chain model. This scalar coefficient is needed to update the environmental objective consistently during the outer-loop coupling. Therefore, EI99 was used as an aggregated single-score screening indicator for optimization and relative comparison among process–supply chain configurations evaluated under the same inventory boundary, functional basis, and modeling structure [15].

More recent LCIA methods, such as ReCiPe, can provide midpoint and endpoint indicators and can also be aggregated into single-score results when normalization and weighting are applied [33]. However, that aggregation requires additional methodological choices regarding midpoint or endpoint level, perspective, normalization, weighting, and category prioritization. In this work, EI99 was retained to provide a consistent single-score objective for optimization, not to replace a full ReCiPe-, GREET-, GWP100-, or CORSIA-compatible life cycle assessment [15,19,20,33,34].

The EI99 results should therefore not be interpreted as regulatory carbon intensity values and do not represent CORSIA eligibility, GREET carbon intensity, ASTM fuel certification, or pathway-specific greenhouse gas certification requirements [5,15,19,20,33,34]. If ReCiPe or a comparable current LCIA method were used, the absolute environmental scores and category-level interpretation would change. In particular, hydrogen consumption, steam and electricity demand, and regional biomass transportation could receive greater visibility in midpoint categories such as climate change, fossil resource scarcity, particulate matter formation, and acidification. Nevertheless, the main methodological conclusion is expected to remain valid: process-level coefficients such as SAF yield, hydrogen demand, utility intensity, environmental burden, and feasible capacity must be propagated into the supply chain model because they affect the environmental ranking of SAF deployment alternatives.

The initial design parameters, cost assumptions, environmental factors, Aspen Plus stream summary, and environmental metric boundary are reported in Sections S3, S4 and S9 of the Supplementary Materials. The process-level environmental burden was evaluated using Eco-indicator 99 (EI99) as a single-score screening metric suitable for multiobjective optimization. EI99 was selected because it provides a scalar environmental objective that can be consistently exchanged between the Aspen Plus–DETL process block and the MILP supply chain model. The EI99 inventory includes electricity, steam, cooling utilities, hydrogen, construction materials, and relevant organic emissions associated with the process model [15].

The EI99 score was used only to compare relative environmental trends among alternative process–supply chain configurations. It should not be interpreted as a regulatory carbon intensity value or as evidence of ASTM, CORSIA, or pathway-specific greenhouse gas certification. Therefore, the EI99 results do not replace a full life cycle assessment based on CORSIA, GREET, ReCiPe, GWP100, or other pathway-specific SAF certification methods. A detailed interpretation of the environmental metric boundary is provided in Section S9 of the Supplementary Materials [5,15,19,20,33,34].

2.6. DETL-Based Process Optimization

The intensified ATJ process model was optimized using Differential Evolution with Tabu List (DETL). This method was selected because the Aspen Plus model defines a nonlinear, nonconvex, simulation-based optimization problem. Gradient information is not directly available, and some candidate designs may fail to converge near infeasible operating regions. Differential Evolution (DE) is suitable for this type of continuous global optimization because it uses mutation, crossover, and selection operators without requiring derivative information [35]. The tabu list extension follows the tabu search (TS) framework [36] and was included to discourage the search from revisiting recently explored regions, improving diversification in constrained process-optimization problems [37].

For each individual r at generation g, a mutant vector is generated as follows:

v r , g = z a , g + F z b , g − z c , g

(33)

where z a , g , z b , g , and z c , g are randomly selected population members, and F is the mutation factor. Binomial crossover is then applied to generate the trial vector:

u r , m , g = u r , m , g , i f r a n d m ≤ C R o r m = m r a n d z r , m , g , o t h e r w i s e

(34)

where CR is the crossover probability, m is the variable index, and m r a n d ensures that at least one variable is inherited from the mutant vector.

Selection is performed according to the following:

z r , g + 1 = u r , g , i f Φ u r , g ≤ Φ z r , g a n d u r , g ∉ T z r , g , o t h e r w i s e

(35)

where T is the tabu list and Φ(z) is the penalized objective function. For each Aspen Plus evaluation, infeasible or nonconvergent simulations are penalized as follows:

Φ z = f z + ρ 1 V i n e q z + ρ 2 V e q z + ρ 3 Ω c o n v z

(36)

where f ( z ) is the economic or environmental objective, V i n e q z and V e q z are inequality and equality constraint-violation measures, Ω c o n v z is a binary penalty for Aspen nonconvergence, and ρ 1 , ρ 2 , and ρ 3 are penalty coefficients.

The DETL algorithm was implemented with a population size of 50, mutation factor F = 0.8, crossover probability CR = 0.9, and a tabu list length of 10. The maximum number of generations was set to 200. The inner process optimization was terminated when the relative improvement in the best objective value was lower than 1 × 10−4 for 20 consecutive generations. To reduce the effect of stochastic variability, each process-optimization case was solved using three independent random seeds, and the best feasible solution was retained. The dispersion among independent runs was recorded to assess the robustness of the process-optimization results. The use of DETL is consistent with process-level numerical optimization studies, in which external optimizers are coupled with detailed process simulators. Such simulator-based optimization is useful when gradients are not directly available, when convergence failures can occur, or when the feasible region is nonlinear and discontinuous. In this work, DETL was therefore assigned to the Aspen Plus process block, whereas the supply chain network was solved by MILP/CPLEX to retain exact optimization of the linear network subproblem.

A hyperparameter sensitivity analysis for the DETL algorithm (detailed in Section S6.2 of the Supplementary Materials) confirmed that the selected base settings provided a practical balance between computational efficiency and global search accuracy, as higher-search configurations produced only marginal improvements in process performance, while significantly increasing execution time.

2.7. MILP–Aspen Plus–DETL Coupling Strategy

The supply chain MILP and the Aspen Plus–DETL process model were linked through an iterative decomposition strategy. At each outer iteration (n), the MILP first solves the supply chain problem using the current process-performance coefficients. The resulting production target and feed conditions are then sent to the Aspen Plus–DETL block. The proposed coupling should be interpreted as an iterative sequential decomposition strategy, not as a fully simultaneous mixed-integer nonlinear optimization formulation. At each outer iteration, the MILP is solved with fixed process-performance coefficients, and the Aspen Plus–DETL block is then solved under the production target and feed conditions generated by the MILP solution. The updated process coefficients are subsequently returned to the MILP. Therefore, the framework seeks consistency between network-level decisions and process-level performance, rather than solving all supply chain and process-design variables in a single monolithic optimization problem.

The network-derived boundary conditions are defined as follows:

ψ n = { Q t a r g e t , n , F a l c , n , χ f e e d , n }

(37)

where Q t a r g e t , n is the ATJ-range hydrocarbon blendstock production target, F a l c , n is the alcohol-intermediate feed rate, and χ f e e d , n represents the feed composition or quality assumptions imposed by the supply chain solution.

The Aspen Plus–DETL process block then optimizes the intensified ATJ process under these boundary conditions and returns the updated process-performance vector:

θ n = { η A T J , n , c P , n , e P , n , h H 2 , n , u P , n , Q _ P , n , Q ¯ P , n }

(38)

where η A T J , n is the effective ATJ upgrading yield, c P , n is the specific process cost, e P , n is the specific environmental burden, h H 2 , n is the hydrogen requirement, u P , n is the utility intensity, and Q _ P , n and Q ¯ P , n are the minimum and maximum feasible production throughputs.

These process-derived coefficients are inserted into the MILP through the following coupling relationships:

P j t n = η A T J , n F j t a l c

(39)

C j t p r o c , n = c P , n P j t

(40)

E I j t p r o c , n = e P , n P j t

(41)

Q _ P , n τ t Y j ≤ P j t ≤ Q ¯ P , n τ t Y j

(42)

The outer-loop convergence criterion is defined as follows:

Δ n = max T A C n − T A C n − 1 max 1 , T A C n − 1 , E I n − E I n − 1 max 1 , E I n − 1

(43)

Convergence is reached when:

Δ n ≤ 1 × 10 − 4

(44)

The optimality properties of the framework follow from this decomposition. For a fixed vector of process-performance coefficients, the MILP subproblem is solved to the prescribed CPLEX optimality gap. For a fixed production target and feed condition, the Aspen Plus–DETL block provides the best feasible process solution found by the stochastic DETL search under the specified convergence and feasibility criteria. The outer loop therefore converges to a process–supply chain consistent fixed point when the exchanged coefficients and objective indicators change by less than the prescribed tolerance. This procedure does not guarantee the global optimum of a fully simultaneous nonlinear mixed-integer formulation. Instead, it provides a reproducible and computationally tractable consistency solution, in which process coefficients are updated endogenously within the supply chain model.

A maximum of 25 outer iterations was imposed to limit computational time. If Aspen Plus did not converge for a network-derived production target, the corresponding process point was marked as infeasible, penalized during the DETL search, and excluded from the MILP coefficient update.

This procedure updates the MILP with process coefficients obtained from the optimized Aspen Plus model at each outer iteration, as summarized in Figure 3. In this way, the supply chain solution is evaluated using process performance consistent with the production target and feed conditions generated by the network model. In the base-case MILP formulation, a single-biorefinery constraint was imposed to represent a centralized deployment strategy and to isolate the effect of process–supply chain coupling on one dominant production site. This restriction was implemented as s u m j y j = 1 , where y j is the binary variable associated with the activation of candidate biorefinery j . To evaluate the effect of this assumption, an additional relaxation analysis was conducted by replacing this condition with s u m j y j ≤ N b i o m a x , where N b i o m a x was varied from one to three.

2.8. Computational Implementation and Reproducibility Protocol

The integrated framework was implemented using three computational components. The supply chain MILP was formulated in GAMS and solved with CPLEX. The intensified ATJ process was simulated in Aspen Plus. The nonlinear process optimization was carried out with an external DETL algorithm, which called Aspen Plus during the search and retrieved the corresponding process-performance coefficients.

At each coupling iteration, the MILP solution provided the production target and feed conditions for the Aspen Plus–DETL block. The process block then returned updated values of ATJ yield, process cost, environmental burden, hydrogen demand, utility consumption, and feasible capacity bounds. These values were transferred back to the MILP as updated coupling coefficients.

The MILP relative optimality gap was set to 1 × 104. The outer MILP–Aspen Plus–DETL loop used a convergence tolerance of 1 × 104 for both total annualized cost and EI99, with a maximum of 25 outer iterations. The inner DETL optimization used the parameter settings reported in Table A6. Aspen Plus simulations that did not converge, or that produced infeasible mass- or energy-balance results, were penalized and excluded from the feasible solution archive.

All simulations were performed on an Intel Core i7 processor at 3.6 GHz with 32 GB RAM. The computational settings are summarized in the Supplementary Materials. To support reproducibility, the geographic data, logistics parameters, economic assumptions, environmental factors, and Aspen Plus input data used in the case study are provided in Sections S1–S3 of the Supplementary Materials.

To evaluate the robustness of the outer-loop solution, the integrated procedure was also initialized with alternative process-coefficient vectors. The tested initializations included a low-performance case, the base decoupled coefficient set, and a high-performance case. For each initialization, the number of outer iterations, final capacity, selected location, TAC, EI99, and final process-coefficient vector were recorded. The convergence histories and initialization-sensitivity results are reported in Section S6 of the Supplementary Materials.

2.9. Case Study Data and Assumptions

The case study was defined for SAF production in Mexico using second-generation sugarcane bagasse as the lignocellulosic resource and Mexico City Airport as the demand node. The spatial data include biomass-producing regions, harvest center coordinates, candidate biorefinery locations, and the airport market node. These data are reported in Figure S1 and Tables S1–S3 of the Supplementary Materials. The case study structure follows previous work on renewable aviation fuel supply chain design in Mexico, where biomass geography, seasonal availability, facility location, and airport demand were shown to affect optimal network decisions [14,38].

The supply chain model uses a one-year monthly planning horizon. This resolution allows the model to represent seasonal biomass availability, biomass inventory, biomass degradation, production scheduling, and ATJ-range hydrocarbon blendstock distribution. The process model operates on a continuous production basis. The connection between monthly supply chain decisions and continuous process operation is established through the throughput scaling factor τ t .

The following assumptions define the base case:

Sugarcane bagasse is treated as the upstream lignocellulosic resource for ethanol-intermediate production.

Ethanol is used as the representative alcohol intermediate.

The upstream bagasse-to-ethanol section is represented by the effective conversion coefficient β E t O H , which includes pretreatment, enzymatic hydrolysis, fermentation, ethanol recovery, and associated material losses.

The Aspen Plus model represents the downstream ethanol-to-ATJ-range upgrading section, including dehydration, oligomerization, hydrogenation, and fractionation at the level required to generate process-performance coefficients.

The modeled C8–C16-enriched product is reported as an ATJ-range hydrocarbon blendstock. Because residual α-olefins remain in the simulated product cut, it is not designated as certified or compositionally equivalent ATJ-SPK [5].

The reported ATJ-range hydrocarbon blendstock quantities do not imply standalone ASTM or CORSIA certification of the modeled fuel; final qualification requires blending and fuel property compliance, while sustainability eligibility requires pathway-specific life cycle greenhouse gas assessment [5,19,20].

Hydrogen is purchased externally. Hydrogen demand and utility requirements are calculated by the Aspen Plus–DETL block and transferred to the MILP as separate economic coefficients. The direct process cost coefficient excludes purchased hydrogen, steam, electricity, and cooling services. For environmental accounting, however, hydrogen and utility burdens remain internal subcomponents of the aggregate downstream ATJ EI99 coefficient and are not added separately to the system-level environmental objective.

Policy incentives, carbon credits, price volatility, stochastic demand, and land-use-change effects are not included.

Environmental performance is evaluated using Eco-indicator 99 as a screening indicator compatible with the optimization framework.

Initial and final inventory conditions are defined through the inventory policy assumptions reported in the Supplementary Materials.

A deterministic screening sensitivity analysis was included to evaluate the robustness of the integrated solution with respect to key upstream, process, market, and environmental parameters. The parameters varied were the effective bagasse-to-ethanol coefficient, available sugarcane bagasse, hydrogen price or hydrogen cost coefficient, electricity/utility price or utility cost coefficient, SAF demand, and the environmental burden assigned to process utilities. Each parameter was evaluated using low, base, and high values while keeping the remaining parameters at their base-case values. The objective of this analysis was not to perform a full stochastic uncertainty assessment, but to identify which assumptions most influence biomass demand, preferred capacity, TAC, EI99, and the selected deployment region.

Unless otherwise stated, SAF production capacity is reported in tSAF/year, TAC in USD/tSAF, and environmental impact in kPt EI99/tSAF, where 1 kPt corresponds to 1000 EI99 points. Biomass quantities are reported on a dry-mass basis, and the upstream bagasse-to-ethanol coefficient is reported as t EtOH/t dry sugarcane bagasse. All process and supply chain environmental burdens were first calculated as annual EI99 points and subsequently divided by annual SAF production and by 1000. Therefore, every specific environmental result reported in this work uses the same functional unit of 1 t of ATJ-range hydrocarbon blendstock.

The process-only, supply chain-only/decoupled, and integrated configurations retain different system boundaries. The process-only configuration includes the downstream Aspen Plus–DETL ATJ block. The supply chain-only/decoupled configuration includes biomass production, upstream bagasse-to-ethanol processing, logistics, inventory, final product transportation, and a fixed downstream ATJ environmental coefficient. The integrated configuration updates the process and network conditions iteratively through the MILP–Aspen Plus–DETL coupling. Despite these boundary differences, all specific environmental values are expressed using the same unit of kPt EI99/tSAF. The environmental coefficients, unit conversions, numerical component balances, and capacity-dependent EI99 calculations used to generate Figures 4, 6, 8, and 9 are documented in Section S10.1 and Tables S33–S35 of the Supplementary Materials.

3. Results

3.1. Baseline Analysis: Decoupled Supply Chain Optimization

The decoupled supply chain baseline provides the reference case against which the value of the proposed multiscale integration can be evaluated. In this scenario, the intensified ATJ process is represented through fixed performance coefficients, while the MILP model optimizes facility location, biomass allocation, production planning, and product distribution. This structure is consistent with conventional biomass and renewable fuel supply chain models, where spatial and temporal logistics are optimized using fixed conversion yields, costs, and environmental factors [2,14].

Figure 4a shows that increasing production capacity from approximately 80,000 to 490,000 tSAF/year reduces TAC from about 1010 to 340 USD/tSAF, corresponding to an approximate 59% reduction. Figure 4c shows a more moderate environmental response. After aggregating biomass production, upstream processing, transportation, the fixed downstream ATJ coefficient, and inventory contributions on a common functional basis, total EI99 decreases from approximately 1.110 to 1.059 kPt EI99/tSAF. This represents a reduction of approximately 5.23%.

The smaller environmental reduction occurs because biomass production, upstream bagasse-to-ethanol processing, and the downstream ATJ contribution remain approximately proportional to SAF output. Only the inventory-related fixed annual burden is substantially diluted as production capacity increases, while the biomass transport contribution increases moderately because larger capacities require a broader biomass-sourcing region.

The baseline therefore provides a useful reference, but it should not be interpreted as the final system optimum. It shows what the supply chain model would select if the ATJ process behaved as a static conversion block across all production scales. In practical terms, the decoupled formulation favors capacity expansion because it does not account for nonlinear process behavior, intensified unit operating limits, or changes in process performance with throughput. The following sections test whether this conclusion remains valid when the ATJ process is optimized in Aspen Plus–DETL and its updated yield, cost, environmental burden, hydrogen demand, utility consumption, and feasible capacity bounds are returned to the supply chain model.

3.2. Spatial and Temporal Behavior of the Optimal Supply Chain

Figure 5 shows the spatial and temporal configuration obtained for the optimal decoupled SAF supply chain. Figure 5a presents the candidate harvest and biorefinery nodes considered in the Mexican case study, while Figure 5b shows the selected network. Node 43 is chosen as both the harvest area and the biorefinery location, with Mexico City Airport as the final demand node. This result indicates that the model favors a site that balances biomass access with proximity to the main fuel market. In biomass-based SAF systems, facility location is not determined only by feedstock abundance; it also depends on transport distance, production capacity, storage requirements, and demand concentration. Similar location–logistics interactions have been reported in previous renewable aviation fuel supply chain studies for Mexico [14,38].

The temporal biomass profile is shown in Figure 5c. Biomass availability is concentrated in the first part of the planning horizon and decreases sharply during the middle months. The model responds by transporting biomass when it is available and using inventory to maintain production during low-availability periods. Harvest center inventory therefore acts as the upstream buffer of the system. This behavior is consistent with biomass supply chain models in which seasonal availability, degradation, and storage constraints must be represented explicitly to avoid unrealistic production schedules [39,40]. The geographic coordinates and biomass availability data used to build the network are reported in Tables S1–S3 and Figure S1 of the Supplementary Materials.

Figure 5d shows the corresponding ATJ-range hydrocarbon blendstock production, airport transport, demand, and product inventory profiles. Production and transport are higher during the first months, decrease in the middle of the year, and recover toward the end of the planning horizon. Product inventory is mainly accumulated between months 5 and 8, indicating that the model uses finished fuel storage to absorb the mismatch between production and airport demand. Demand remains comparatively stable, around 3.5 × 104–4.4 × 104 t/month, whereas production and shipment vary more strongly. The optimal network therefore relies on two buffers: biomass inventory upstream and ATJ-range hydrocarbon blendstock inventory downstream.

This temporal behavior helps explain the scale effects observed in the decoupled baseline of Figure 4. Under fixed ATJ performance coefficients, the supply chain can reduce unit TAC and EI99 by increasing capacity and smoothing seasonal imbalances through inventory. In the decoupled case, these production profiles are evaluated with constant ATJ performance coefficients. Yield, hydrogen demand, utility consumption, separation performance, and feasible operating limits are assumed to remain unchanged across the capacity range. This provides a clear baseline, but it also defines the main limitation of the decoupled formulation.

Thus, Figure 5 should be interpreted as the optimal logistics response under fixed process-performance assumptions. It shows how the supply chain model coordinates location, biomass transport, storage, production, and airport delivery when the conversion block remains unchanged across operating scales. The integrated framework evaluated in the following sections tests whether this spatial and temporal configuration remains favorable once the Aspen Plus–DETL process model updates yield, cost, environmental burden, hydrogen demand, utility intensity, and feasible capacity bounds.

3.3. Cost and Environmental Contribution Analysis

The relative contributions of biomass, transportation, and biorefinery operations to the total annualized cost (TAC) and environmental impact (EI99) of the decoupled SAF supply chain system are presented in Figure 6. In economic terms, the biorefinery is the largest contributor, accounting for approximately 44.5% of TAC. The upstream biomass block, comprising raw bagasse procurement and the effective upstream conversion contribution represented in the decoupled model, accounts for approximately 30.0% of TAC, followed by solid biomass transportation at 17.0% and liquid fuel transportation at 8.6%. This distribution shows that, under the decoupled formulation, the cost structure is driven mainly by conversion-related expenditures, while final product distribution has a smaller contribution.

This cost distribution is consistent with the spatial and temporal behavior reported in Figure 5. The selected network relies on biomass mobilization and inventory accumulation to compensate for seasonal availability, which explains the relevance of biomass acquisition and solid transportation costs. However, the biorefinery remains the dominant economic block. Once the selected network keeps transport distances within a feasible regional range, improvements in process design and conversion performance have greater leverage on TAC than marginal reductions in liquid fuel distribution costs. Similar behavior has been reported in biomass-based supply chain studies, where conversion and processing costs often dominate the total cost once regional logistics are technically feasible [2,39]. The numerical derivation of these contributions and the internal disaggregation of the downstream ATJ subtotal are reported in Tables S33 and S34 of the Supplementary Materials.

The environmental contribution analysis was performed at the representative production level of 240,000 tSAF/year. The downstream ATJ block contributes 0.558 kPt EI99/tSAF, equivalent to 52.69% of the total environmental burden. Upstream bagasse-to-ethanol processing contributes 0.4198 kPt EI99/tSAF, or 39.64%. Consequently, the combined upstream and downstream conversion system accounts for approximately 92.32% of total EI99. Biomass production, biomass transportation, inventory, and final product transportation collectively account for the remaining 7.68%.

These results show that conversion activities represent the largest environmental contribution, but the downstream ATJ block does not account for 99.99% of total EI99. The logistics and feedstock-related terms remain quantitatively identifiable and are included explicitly in the system-level balance.

This result has a direct implication for the decoupled baseline. The MILP model can represent changes in biomass allocation, transport, storage, production scheduling, and airport distribution. However, when the environmental coefficient of the ATJ process is kept fixed, the model cannot capture changes in process energy demand, hydrogen consumption, utility requirements, or separation performance. Since EI99 is dominated by the biorefinery block, this fixed-coefficient assumption can strongly influence the environmental conclusions obtained from the baseline.

The contribution analysis therefore provides the technical basis for evaluating the intensified ATJ process separately before closing the loop with the supply chain model. Reactive distillation and intensified separation systems have been proposed to reduce utility consumption, equipment count, and thermal inefficiencies relative to conventional process trains [27]. In ATJ systems, intensified configurations have also been shown to improve economic and environmental performance by reducing energy demand and simplifying separation requirements [10,11,12,28]. Accordingly, Figure 6 indicates where the largest sensitivity of the system is located: not in final fuel distribution, but in the process block used to convert the alcohol intermediate into ATJ-range hydrocarbon blendstock.

Taken together, Figure 4, Figure 5 and Figure 6 define the behavior of the decoupled case. The baseline analysis shows that higher production capacity reduces unit TAC and EI99. The spatial–temporal analysis shows that this behavior is supported by biomass and product inventory buffers. The contribution analysis shows that the biorefinery dominates the environmental profile and represents the largest economic contributor. The next step is to determine whether the same cost and environmental trends remain valid when the ATJ process is optimized directly, rather than represented by fixed coefficients.

3.4. Isolated Aspen Plus–DETL Optimization of the Intensified ATJ Process Block

The intensified ATJ process block was optimized separately in Aspen Plus–DETL before being coupled back to the supply chain model. This step evaluates how the downstream ethanol-to-ATJ-range hydrocarbon blendstock section behaves when its design and operating variables are allowed to change, instead of being represented by fixed coefficients. The analysis therefore refers only to the process block, not to the full integrated MILP–Aspen Plus–DETL framework. The process-level results were interpreted together with the literature-normalized benchmark reported in Section S5. This benchmark provides context for the reactive distillation-based configuration by comparing it with a base distributed ATJ process for Mexico, a conventional ATJ/ETJ reference, and previous intensified ATJ configurations. Therefore, the isolated Aspen Plus–DETL results should be read as the behavior of the intensified downstream ATJ block, whereas the decoupled and integrated MILP cases should be read as system-level optimization scenarios. The reactive distillation configuration, Aspen Plus simulation setup, and product-stream compositions used in this process-level optimization are reported in Figure S3 and Tables S7 and S8 of the Supplementary Materials.

The TAC–EI99 region obtained for the isolated ATJ process block is shown in Figure 7a. At environmental impacts above approximately 0.75 kPt Ecopoints/ t S A F , TAC remains within a relatively narrow range of about 790–850 USD/ t S A F . Outside this region, TAC increases sharply and reaches values above 1150 USD/ t S A F . This behavior indicates that the intensified ATJ process does not follow a simple linear economic–environmental trade-off. The coupled reaction–separation structure creates operating regions where small changes in design variables can produce large cost penalties.

The capacity trends in Figure 7b,c show the same process-level nonlinearity. In Figure 7b, TAC remains near 1140–1150 USD at capacities below roughly (150 × 103) t S A F /year. Above approximately (200 × 103) t S A F /year, TAC decreases to about 840 USD/ t S A F . Figure 7c shows a stronger environmental response, with EI99 decreasing from nearly 1.7 to 0.55 kPt Ecopoints/ t S A F , equivalent to an approximate 68% reduction. Higher throughput therefore improves equipment utilization and distributes fixed environmental burdens more effectively, but only after the process reaches a favorable operating range.

This process-level behavior contrasts with the decoupled baseline shown in Figure 4. In the baseline, increasing capacity appeared consistently favorable because ATJ yield, specific cost, and environmental burden were fixed across all production scales. The Aspen Plus–DETL results show that this assumption is restrictive for the intensified ATJ block. Process performance changes with throughput, reaction–separation interactions, utility demand, hydrogen consumption, equipment sizing, and feasible operating conditions. The smooth economies of scale observed in the decoupled supply chain model should therefore be interpreted as a baseline result obtained under fixed process assumptions, rather than as a final system-level conclusion.

The solution pattern also supports the use of a derivative-free optimizer. The Aspen Plus ATJ model behaves as a simulation-based problem with strong variable interactions and possible convergence failures near infeasible operating regions. Differential Evolution is appropriate for nonlinear continuous global optimization, while the tabu list mechanism improves search diversification by discouraging returns to recently explored solutions. This is consistent with the use of DETL for constrained chemical engineering optimization problems with nonconvex search spaces and difficult convergence behavior.

The isolated process results also explain the environmental dominance of the biorefinery reported in Figure 6. Since EI99 changes strongly with process capacity and operating conditions, fixing the process environmental coefficient removes the main source of variability from the supply chain model. For this reason, the ATJ process block should not be treated only as a static conversion coefficient when evaluating SAF deployment at the system level. The integrated optimization in the following section uses the Aspen Plus–DETL outputs to update yield, cost, environmental burden, hydrogen demand, utility intensity, and feasible capacity within the MILP model.

3.5. Integrated MILP–Aspen Plus–DETL Optimization of the SAF System

The integrated MILP–Aspen Plus–DETL optimization evaluates the SAF system after closing the loop between the supply chain model and the intensified ATJ process block. In this configuration, the MILP determines biomass allocation, facility location, production planning, inventory, and airport delivery, while the Aspen Plus–DETL block updates the process coefficients used by the network model. These coefficients include ATJ yield, specific cost, environmental burden, hydrogen demand, utility intensity, and feasible capacity bounds. The results therefore represent the coupled system response, rather than the isolated behavior of either the supply chain or the process model.

The TAC–EI99 relationship obtained for the integrated framework is shown in Figure 8a. TAC increases from approximately 3400 to 6800 USD/ t S A F as the environmental impact increases from about 0.77 to 1.31 kPt Ecopoints/ t S A F . This trend differs from the isolated ATJ process behavior shown in Figure 7a, where the Pareto region had a more irregular structure. Once network feasibility, production requirements, and process-performance updates are considered simultaneously, the economic–environmental space becomes more strongly shaped by the cost of satisfying regional demand under feasible ATJ operating conditions.

The larger TAC values obtained in the integrated case are mainly explained by the broader system boundary used in this calculation. The isolated Aspen Plus–DETL case evaluates the downstream ATJ process block, whereas the integrated TAC includes biomass acquisition, inbound biomass transportation, biomass inventory, annualized biorefinery capacity, process operating and equipment costs, ATJ-range hydrocarbon blendstock inventory, and final product transportation to the airport demand node. In addition, the integrated model uses process coefficients that are recalculated under the production targets imposed by the network, including ATJ yield, hydrogen demand, utility intensity, environmental burden, and feasible capacity limits. Therefore, the integrated TAC should be interpreted as a system-level unit cost, not as a plant-only process cost. The revised integrated cost decomposition separates raw material purchase from upstream conversion and distinguishes the direct downstream ATJ coefficient from purchased hydrogen and utilities. Raw bagasse acquisition contributes 206.95 USD/tSAF, consistent with the documented feed requirement and bagasse price, whereas upstream pretreatment, enzymatic hydrolysis, fermentation, and ethanol recovery contribute 913.05 USD/tSAF. The direct ATJ and hydrogen-and-utility terms are reported as non-overlapping contributions. The complete component-level reconciliation reproducing the integrated TAC of 5100 USD/tSAF is provided in Table S21.

The integrated framework identifies a production-capacity region between approximately 120,000 and 300,000 tSAF/year. Across this interval, total EI99 decreases from approximately 0.77 to 1.31 kPt EI99/tSAF. The integrated base case at 200,000 tSAF/year has a total environmental burden of 1.063 kPt EI99/tSAF.

The integrated EI99 values were calculated using the same environmental components and functional unit applied to the decoupled configuration. This eliminates the previous difference in numerical scale between the fixed process coefficient, the isolated ATJ results, and the system-level environmental objective.

This result modifies the interpretation of the decoupled baseline in Figure 4. In the baseline, increasing capacity appeared uniformly favorable because yield, energy use, hydrogen demand, cost, and environmental burden were fixed. The isolated ATJ optimization in Figure 7 showed that process performance is nonlinear and depends on operating conditions. The integrated results in Figure 8 combine both effects: the model still benefits from scale, but the system-level region shifts to higher TAC and EI99 values because process performance is updated inside the supply chain calculation, rather than imposed as a static coefficient.

At the representative decoupled operating point, the downstream ATJ block accounts for 52.7% of total EI99, while the complete upstream and downstream conversion system accounts for 92.3%. Therefore, process-level performance remains environmentally important, but biomass production, transportation, and inventory contributions are not negligible and are explicitly retained in the system balance.

The comparison with previous integrated biorefinery studies is relevant because it clarifies the pathway- and region-specific contribution of this work. Galanopoulos et al. [6] showed that linking supply chain optimization with Aspen-based process evaluation can improve the realism of biorefinery assessments. The present case extends that approach to an intensified ATJ pathway for SAF production in Mexico, where regional biomass availability, airport demand, and process feasibility are evaluated within the same iterative framework. The resulting operating region would not be obtained by optimizing the supply chain first and evaluating the process afterward, or by optimizing the ATJ process without the network constraints.

Overall, the integrated optimization provides a more conservative system-level estimate than the isolated models. The supply chain-only formulation favors high production capacities because it assumes invariant process performance. The process-only optimization identifies favorable ATJ operating regions without accounting for regional biomass logistics, inventory, and demand satisfaction. The integrated formulation balances both requirements. It selects solutions that remain feasible for the supply chain while using ATJ process coefficients that respond to production scale and operating conditions. This supports the main result of the study: SAF deployment from sugarcane bagasse-derived alcohol intermediates should be evaluated with process and supply chain decisions coupled, rather than optimized independently.

3.6. Comparison of Optimization Strategies and Multiscale Interaction

The comparison among the three optimization strategies shows how the system response changes when process and supply chain decisions are solved separately or coupled within the same framework. The three cases represent different modeling levels: process-only optimization evaluates the intensified ATJ block without regional logistics, supply chain-only optimization evaluates the network using fixed process coefficients, and integrated optimization updates the process coefficients inside the MILP model.

The production-capacity distributions are shown in Figure 9a. The process-only optimization occupies the lowest capacity range, approximately (70–200 × 103) t S A F /year. This range reflects the operating scale at which the intensified ATJ process can reduce TAC and EI99 without being constrained by regional biomass supply, inventory, or airport demand. The supply chain-only case moves to a higher capacity range, approximately 320–490 × 103 t S A F /year, because fixed process coefficients allow the MILP to benefit from network-level economies of scale. The integrated case falls between both regions, approximately 120–300 × 103 t S A F /year. This intermediate range indicates that process feasibility limits the high-capacity solutions preferred by the network, while regional demand and logistics prevent the process from remaining at its smallest favorable scale.

The TAC–EI99 solution regions in Figure 9b confirm this separation. The process-only solutions remain in a low-impact region, with TAC values close to 840–1150 USD/tSAF and EI99 values, between approximately 0.47 and 0.63 kPt EI99/tSAF. The supply chain-only solutions operate under distinct trade-offs, with TAC values spanning from 340 to 1010 USD/tSAF and their EI99 values extending across a higher range of approximately 0.95 to 1.33 kPt EI99/tSAF due to the simplified nature of the fixed process coefficients. In contrast, the integrated solutions form a separate compromise region, with TAC strictly bounded between approximately 3400 and 6800 USD/ t S A F and EI99 between 0.78 and 1.31 kPt Ecopoints/ t S A F .

The harmonized TAC–EI99 comparison in Figure 9b shows that the process-only configuration spans the broadest environmental interval, approximately 0.47–0.63 kPt EI99/tSAF, because its performance changes nonlinearly with process scale and operating conditions. The decoupled system occupies a narrower system-level interval of approximately 0.95–1.33 kPt EI99/tSAF. The integrated solutions lie between approximately 0.78 and 1.31 kPt EI99/tSAF.

Unlike the previous representation, the corrected environmental regions are not separated by an order of magnitude. The decoupled and integrated regions partially overlap because both now include the same upstream, logistics, process, inventory, and distribution components. The principal effect of multiscale coupling is therefore observed in the selected capacity region, process feasibility, and TAC, rather than in an artificial difference caused by inconsistent environmental scaling.

This separation is the main evidence of multiscale interaction. The integrated solution is not obtained by inserting the process optimum into the supply chain model, nor by evaluating the supply chain optimum afterward in Aspen Plus. It is obtained by allowing the network and process blocks to exchange production targets, feed conditions, yield, cost, environmental burden, hydrogen demand, utility intensity, and feasible capacity bounds. As a result, the integrated framework identifies a compromise region, where process-level nonlinearities and network-level requirements are both active.

The higher TAC and EI99 values in the integrated region should therefore be interpreted as a more complete system estimate, not as poorer model performance. The process-only case excludes logistics and demand constraints. The supply chain-only case excludes changes in ATJ performance with throughput and operating conditions. The integrated case includes both effects. This explains why its solution region shifts toward higher cost and environmental impact: it internalizes process feasibility, biomass logistics, production planning, storage, and airport demand within the same iterative calculation.

The comparison also clarifies the roles of the previous results. Figure 4 showed that the decoupled supply chain model favors capacity expansion when ATJ performance is fixed. Figure 5 showed that this network behavior relies on spatial selection and temporal buffering through biomass and product inventories. Figure 6 showed that the biorefinery dominates the environmental contribution, making fixed process coefficients a critical assumption. Figure 7 showed that the intensified ATJ block is nonlinear and scale-dependent. Figure 8 then showed the behavior of the coupled MILP–Aspen Plus–DETL system. Figure 9 brings these results together and shows that the coupled solution occupies a distinct operating region.

This result extends previous SAF supply chain studies for Mexico, where biomass availability, logistics, facility location, and airport demand were optimized, while process performance remained external to the network model. The present framework keeps those supply chain decisions, but conditions them on the feasibility and performance of the intensified ATJ process. The methodological contribution is therefore the endogenous updating of ATJ yield, cost, environmental burden, hydrogen demand, utility intensity, and capacity bounds within the supply chain optimization. This supports the central result of the study: SAF deployment from sugarcane bagasse-derived alcohol intermediates cannot be reliably evaluated by optimizing the supply chain and the intensified ATJ process independently.

The integrated MILP–Aspen Plus–DETL framework reached convergence within the maximum number of outer iterations imposed in the computational protocol. The convergence history reported in Figure S4 shows the evolution of the main exchanged indicators, including ATJ yield, process cost, EI99, hydrogen demand, utility intensity, TAC, and total EI99. The largest changes occurred during the first outer iterations, when the fixed decoupled coefficients were replaced by process coefficients consistent with the network-derived production target. Subsequent iterations produced progressively smaller changes until the convergence tolerance was satisfied.

The initialization-sensitivity results in Table S17 indicate that the final integrated solution was not driven by a single arbitrary initial coefficient vector. Although different initializations produced different early-iteration trajectories, the final capacity region and selected location remained stable within the tested range. This supports the use of the iterative framework as a process–supply chain consistency procedure. Nevertheless, the solution should be interpreted as a converged fixed point of the decomposition strategy, not as a guaranteed global optimum of a fully simultaneous MINLP formulation.

A screening sensitivity analysis was performed to evaluate the influence of key assumptions on the integrated solution. The tested parameters included the effective bagasse-to-ethanol coefficient, available sugarcane bagasse, hydrogen cost, utility cost, SAF demand, and environmental burden associated with process utilities. These parameters were selected because they affect either the upstream ethanol-intermediate availability, the downstream ATJ process coefficients, or the system-level economic and environmental objectives.

The sensitivity results are summarized in Table S20 and Figure S6. The effective bagasse-to-ethanol coefficient mainly affected biomass demand and feedstock pressure, whereas hydrogen and utility costs affected the process cost contribution to TAC. The environmental burden assigned to utilities affected EI99 more strongly than TAC, reflecting the dominant contribution of the biorefinery/process block to the environmental objective. SAF demand affected the production scale and, therefore, the balance between economies of scale, biomass logistics, and process feasibility.

Across the evaluated range, the integrated solution remained within the intermediate-capacity region identified in the base case. However, the objective values were sensitive to upstream yield and utility-related assumptions. This confirms that the integrated framework should be interpreted as a decision support model whose conclusions depend on clearly stated feedstock, process, market, and environmental assumptions. A full stochastic or robust optimization formulation is outside the scope of the present work, but is a natural extension of the proposed framework.

To further support the visual interpretation of these structural changes without the distortion of different physical units and absolute scales, a multi-objective dimensionless comparison is provided in Figure 10. This normalized view maps the behavior of both the decoupled baseline and the integrated framework relative to a common reference point. While the decoupled baseline operates closely around the unitary reference ( q s ∗ = 1.0 ), the endogenous propagation of process-level nonlinearities and regional supply chain restrictions triggers an explicit contraction in the feasible production capacity alongside a significant escalation in the normalized TAC. This graphic representation complements the absolute regions previously discussed by illustrating that the integrated solution represents an entirely different modeling boundary, rather than a simple rescaling of the decoupled behavior. To support these structural modifications with granular, process-level evidence and satisfy specific model differentiation and validation requirements, a direct side-by-side comparison of the stream flows, operating parameters, and multi-scale metrics between the standalone optimized ATJ process and the integrated supply chain-process configuration is provided in Section S12 of the Supplementary Materials. Within this section, Table S37 presents the mass flow rates of key chemical streams within the reactive distillation column, Table S38 contrasts the specific design parameters identified by the DETL algorithm under both modeling boundaries, and Table S39 outlines the disaggregated economic and environmental performance metrics that confirm the multi-scale compromise of the coupled framework.

4. Discussion

The results show that SAF system design changes when supply chain decisions and intensified ATJ process performance are evaluated within the same optimization framework. In the decoupled baseline, increasing production capacity reduced unit TAC and EI99 because the MILP model benefited from economies of scale, facility utilization, and temporal inventory coordination. This behavior was useful as a reference case, but it relied on fixed ATJ yield, cost, hydrogen demand, utility consumption, and environmental coefficients. The isolated Aspen Plus–DETL process optimization then showed that the intensified ATJ block does not behave as a static conversion unit. Its performance changed nonlinearly with throughput, operating conditions, and reaction–separation interactions. When both levels were coupled, the feasible solution region moved to an intermediate capacity range, confirming that process performance affects the interpretation of supply chain optimality.

This behavior is consistent with the enterprise-wide optimization perspective proposed by Grossmann [9]. Supply, production, conversion, and distribution decisions should be coordinated when interactions across decision levels affect system performance. In the present case, the supply chain-only model favored higher capacities because process coefficients were fixed, while the process-only model identified lower-capacity regions that were attractive from a plant-level perspective, but did not include regional biomass logistics or airport demand. The integrated formulation balanced both effects. As a result, it produced more conservative estimates of TAC and EI99, but these estimates are more representative of a system in which biomass supply, process feasibility, production scale, and demand satisfaction are active at the same time.

The findings also refine the interpretations of previous biomass and renewable fuel supply chain studies. García and You [2] showed that supply chain design is critical in process industries because resource availability, transportation, and capacity decisions are strongly linked. For Mexico, studies such as Domínguez-García et al. [38] and Matos-Ríos et al. [14] demonstrated that biomass geography, facility location, hydrogen supply, and airport demand influence renewable aviation fuel networks. Those studies provided a strong basis for SAF supply chain planning, but process performance was mainly treated as an external input. The present work extends that approach by showing that the ATJ process block is not only a source of parameters. It is a decision-dependent subsystem whose yield, cost, hydrogen demand, utility consumption, and environmental burden can change the preferred production scale.

The spatial and temporal results support this interpretation. The optimal decoupled network relied on biomass inventory upstream and ATJ-range hydrocarbon blendstock inventory downstream to buffer seasonal feedstock availability and comparatively stable airport demand. This confirms the value of multiperiod MILP formulations for biomass-based fuel systems, where storage, degradation, and production scheduling must be represented explicitly. However, the same result also exposes a limitation of logistics-only optimization. Inventory can make the supply chain feasible at the network level, but the ATJ process must still operate efficiently under the resulting production profile. This is particularly relevant for SAF systems, where feedstock availability, logistics, production cost, and policy requirements remain major barriers to scale up.

The contribution analysis provides the strongest justification for coupling the intensified ATJ process with the supply chain model. The biorefinery represented the largest economic contributor and dominated the EI99 profile. Transportation and biomass logistics were still relevant, especially for TAC, but their environmental contribution was small relative to the process block. This means that the main source of environmental variability comes from process-level performance. If the process environmental coefficient is fixed, the supply chain model cannot capture the dominant driver of EI99. The integrated framework addresses this limitation by updating process yield, cost, hydrogen demand, utility intensity, environmental burden, and feasible capacity bounds during optimization.

The process-level results are consistent with the ATJ and process-intensification literature. Romero-Izquierdo et al. SHANGHAI, Aug. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- On August 17, Shanghai Electric Company (SEHK: 02727, SSE: 601727) partnered with Shanghai International Port Group and CMA CGM Group to conduct a biomethanol bunkering operation with a total volume of 8,000 metric tons, the largest single biomethanol bunkering operation on record. The bunkering ceremony at Shanghai Yangshan Port was titled "Green Fueled Globe, Lead the Future".

The principal biomethanol supplier for this operation was Shanghai Electric's Taonan green methanol project. This operation not only marks a significant breakthrough in supply volume but also indicates that the Taonan project is fulfilling stable production and large-scale deliveries.

Behind this success lies a fully connected interprovincial green fuel supply chain that serves as the core support. At the Shanghai International Shipping Green Fuel Sustainable‑Development Conference held on June 30 this year, Shanghai, Jilin and Liaoning officially launched the joint‑built green‑fuel transportation corridor. It establishes the north‑to‑south methanol shipment route: production at the Taonan project in Jilin, transit and storage at Dalian Port and final bunkering at Shanghai Port.

As the core production capacity base of the transportation corridor, Shanghai Electric's Taonan green methanol project draws on Jilin's abundant local wind and solar resources as well as biomass feedstock. Deploying independently‑developed full‑set process systems and core equipment, the facility is the world's first large‑scale plant manufacturing biomethanol by combining green electricity and biomass. It meets the ship‑bunkering requirements of Shanghai's International Shipping Center and provides crucial support for the development of the three major green‑fuel centers for international shipping.

Shanghai Electric will continue to focus on the complete industrial chain covering the production, storage, transportation and application of diversified green fuels. The company will intensify research into pivotal core‑technologies and continuously upgrade its integrated green fuel solution chain. Driving industrial advancement through technology‑driven innovation, Shanghai Electric cooperates with partners to accelerate construction on the integrated green-hydrogen-coupled-biomass gasification Green-Methanol and Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) project (Taonan Phase-II). The company will steadily improve its large‑scale green‑fuel supply capacity for the aviation and maritime sectors. Shanghai Electric shall further devote itself to fulfilling China's national dual‑carbon goals and galvanizing the worldwide shift to low‑carbon clean energy.

title: APAC to account for 55% of global biopower capacity by 2035, forecasts GlobalData
description:
The Asia-Pacific (APAC) region is forecast to increase its share of global biopower capacity from around 42% in 2025 to roughly 55% by 2035, says GlobalData, a leading intelligence and productivity platform.
GlobalData’s latest report, “Biopower Market, Update 2026 – Global Market Outlook, Trends, and Key Country Analysis” reveals that China held the largest cumulative biopower capacity in APAC at 47.4GW in 2025 and is estimated to account for more than half of all forecast additions over the period.
Europe followed, with around 28% of global capacity in 2025, expanding modestly as its established fleet approached saturation.
North America was the only region to record a decline in installed capacity during 2020-25, as retirements outpaced new build.
Solid biofuels made up the largest share of global biopower capacity in 2025, followed by renewable municipal waste and biogas.
text:
The global biopower sector has seen its growth shift in recent years, with a small number of Asian markets accounting for the majority of new capacity while several countries in Europe and North America restructure their support frameworks. The Asia-Pacific (APAC) region is forecast to increase its share of global biopower capacity from around 42% in 2025 to roughly 55% by 2035, says GlobalData, a leading intelligence and productivity platform.

GlobalData’s latest report, “Biopower Market, Update 2026 – Global Market Outlook, Trends, and Key Country Analysis” reveals that China held the largest cumulative biopower capacity in APAC at 47.4GW in 2025 and is estimated to account for more than half of all forecast additions over the period. Europe followed, with around 28% of global capacity in 2025, expanding modestly as its established fleet approached saturation. North America was the only region to record a decline in installed capacity during 2020-25, as retirements outpaced new build.

Mohammed Ziauddin, Power Analyst at GlobalData, comments: “Rising urban waste volumes, the availability of agricultural residues, and the value of dispatchable renewable generation in grids with high solar and wind penetration continue to support investment in the sector. Growth in several Asian markets is increasingly supported by locally available agricultural residues and municipal waste, particularly in China, which has developed one of the world’s largest waste-to-energy fleets.”

Renewable municipal waste accounted for over 40% of China’s biopower capacity in 2025, providing both a feedstock for power generation and a waste treatment service, while residue-based projects similarly draw on by-products of large agricultural and processing industries. Projects of this type can have economic drivers beyond electricity revenues, including waste treatment fees and integrated access to low-cost residues, although policy support remains important across all these markets.

Policy support for conventional biomass power has become more selective across several mature markets, with incentives increasingly directed toward applications offering additional system value. Japan announced that new woody biomass plants of 10MW or more using general timber will no longer be covered by feed-in-tariff and feed-in premium support from FY2026, while smaller and waste-based facilities remain eligible. South Korea’s December 2024 reform of Renewable Energy Certificate (REC) support ended eligibility for new biomass plants and phased down weightings for state-owned facilities, while retaining support for domestically sourced biomass.

In the UK, a new low-carbon, dispatchable Contract for Difference for the country’s largest converted biomass plant caps the annual subsidised load factor at 27% from 2027, substantially below its previous operating profile, and pays the plant to generate when the system requires it. Germany is transitioning a large existing biogas fleet from guaranteed remuneration toward competitive tendering, with around 3,000 plants reaching the end of their 20-year support contracts by 2030.

Ziauddin adds: “Support for conventional biomass electricity is being restructured rather than removed in the markets where the sector was first established. Policy is increasingly assessing what additional value a given application provides, whether that is dispatchable capacity, useful heat, waste treatment, or renewable gas, rather than treating all biomass generation equally. This is reshaping which projects proceed rather than reducing the role of bioenergy overall.”

Feedstock composition also varies by market. Solid biofuels made up the largest share of global biopower capacity in 2025, followed by renewable municipal waste and biogas. Brazil and Thailand draw primarily on bagasse from their sugar industries, the US and the Nordic countries on black liquor and wood residues from pulp and paper production, while Germany and Italy rely largely on agricultural biogas.

Ziauddin concludes: “The trajectory of the biopower market over the next decade will depend on three factors: feedstock security, the design of support mechanisms, and the system value a project delivers beyond electricity alone. Competition for sustainable biomass is increasing as biomethane, sustainable aviation fuel, and industrial heat draw on overlapping feedstock pools, while import-dependent markets remain exposed to price and sustainability pressures in the pellet trade.

“Countries with domestic residue availability and integrated waste management systems are better positioned to sustain growth, and frameworks that reward dispatchability, heat recovery, and waste treatment alongside generation are likely to determine where new capacity is built.”

title: Neste has delivered sustainable aviation fuel to Emirates - Travel Report

text:
From January 2027, the Swiss CO2 Act requires airlines and travel sellers of flights operating to/from Switzerland to provide transparent, standardized CO₂ emissions information for passenger air travel.

Implementing transparency and comparability for travelers will not be easy for the industry, given multiple methodologies, fragmented data sources, and integration challenges that have historically limited consistency.

A New Requirement for Emissions Disclosure in Switzerland

The Swiss CO2 Act creates new compliance challenges for aviation stakeholders.

It applies broadly across the value chain, covering airlines, travel agents, and any organization offering flights to and from Switzerland, these stakeholders must ensure that emissions information is presented clearly, visibly, and consistently as part of flight information. In addition, airlines are obliged to make the emissions data available to their partners who enable the sale of airlines’ flights.

The regulation aims to strengthen credibility, transparency, and passenger trust.

Official guidance published by the Swiss Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN) provides further detail, with implementation guidance available in English, French, and German.

IATA CO2 Connect: A Trusted Industry Foundation

To meet the new requirements in Switzerland, the industry is turning to a shared solution.

IATA CO2 Connect helps organizations address these challenges and makes it easier for airlines and travel sellers to comply with the new regulation.

Built on real airline operational data and already embedded within key industry systems, IATA CO2 Connect enables aligned, scalable regulatory compliance across the travel ecosystem.

The solution provides a standardized approach to calculating per-passenger CO₂ emissions, built directly on airline operational data. Unlike traditional models that rely on averages, it reflects real-world conditions: aircraft type, fuel burn, load factors, and cabin configuration to produce more accurate and consistent results. It is also the first calculator to account for sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), which will play an increasing role in fuel supply in the coming years. Currently, 113 airlines are contributing data with fuel burn to the platform.

Developed by IATA in collaboration with airlines, the methodology is aligned with recognized industry frameworks, including IATA Recommended Practice 1726 and ISO standards, ensuring global consistency and methodological rigor.

Today, it is used across the travel ecosystem by airlines, technology providers, and travel sellers, forming one trusted source of emissions data for the industry.

With IATA CO2 Connect can provide airlines and travel resellers with the industry’s most accurate emissions data either through direct access to IATA CO2 Connect or through integrations across Amadeus, Chooose, and ATPCO.

A Collaborative Model for Airlines

Collaboration is at the heart of IATA CO2 Connect.

Through a “give-to-get” model, airlines contribute key operational data and in return receive access to CO₂ emissions calculations at no cost.

This data can then be accessed via APIs or flat files, enabling airlines to:

Display emissions on their own websites such as PLUSULTRA

Share data with partners and distribution channels, and

Support regulatory compliance, including the Swiss CO₂ Act.

The result is a continuously improving system, where industry participation directly enhances accuracy and consistency.

For information on how the airlines can contribute to IATA CO2 Connect and make use of the “give to get” model, reach out to us.

Meeting of the data sharing requirement via CO2 Connect

Per the Swiss CO₂ Act, airlines are obliged to make their emissions data available to all parties offering their flights to/from Switzerland for sale, although the exact mechanism is not prescribed in the regulation. Participating in IATA CO2 Connect by sharing their operational data, which is then made available via IATA for all third parties, satisfies this requirement.

Seamless Integration Across Existing Platforms

A key advantage of IATA CO2 Connect is that it does not require new systems to be built from scratch. Instead, it is already integrated into the platforms airlines and travel sellers use every day.

Amadeus: Embedded in core travel workflows

IATA CO2 Connect data is integrated in Amadeus core products like Master Pricer and Flex Pricer (shopping APIs), Selling Platform Connect (front-end for Travel Sellers), Cytric (self-booking tool for TMCs & Corporations), Dynamic Travel Documents and in many other areas/products, with the last part of the integration roadmap to be completed in the coming months.

This integration enables emissions data to be displayed directly within search results, journey bookings, and corporate travel management solutions.

For airlines and travel agents already using Amadeus that wish to access IATA CO2 Connect data and request access to it, this means for the Amadeus Products already integrated, a rapid activation with minimal disruption, leveraging existing workflows rather than introducing new ones.

As the ecosystem evolves, additional availability, including through Navitaire, is expected to further expand access.

Through its partnership with IATA, Chooose integrates IATA CO2 Connect data into customer-facing experiences.

The process is straightforward. IATA calculates CO₂ emissions based on operational airline data, which are then integrated into Chooose solutions. From there, emissions information is delivered directly to airline consumer and corporate customers through booking flows, web applications, and business portals. At the same time, Chooose enables airlines to present this information in a clear, engaging format helping customers understand their emissions impact.

text:
The U.K. Environment Agency on Aug. 14 formally granted Drax Power Ltd. a permit change that will allow carbon capture to be implemented at Drax Power Station. Drax first applied for the permit variation in May 2023.

The U.K. Environment Agency in late May issued a draft decision proposing to grant Drax the permit change. A public comment period was open through June 24. The agency has now formally approved the permit variation.

“The decision is based on Drax demonstrating that it has met and will continue to meet expected mandatory conditions as outlined in the permit,” the U.K. Environment Agency said in a statement. Thea agency said it only issues permits or permit variations if its satisfied that the operator can comply with the permit conditions and has appropriate systems in place to operate without causing harm to the environment, human health or wildlife.

“We have reviewed the comments and evidence from the consultation into our draft decision and are satisfied that robust levels of environmental protection are met,” said Ian Foster, area environment manager at the Environment Agency. “Environmental law sets out these conditions, and as a regulator we will issue the permit if we can find no reason that the operator would not be able to comply.”

Drax applied for the permit variation in May 2023, with initial public consultations held in 2023 and 2025. The permit variation now allows Drax Power Station to add a post combustion carbon capture system (PCC). As part of project, the company would replace the existing effluent treatment plant associated with flue gas desulphurization with a new treatment plant for treatment of effluent from the quencher tower. Drax would also modify the flue gas layout and abatement units of units five and six, install a quencher tower to treat flue gasses prior to PCC, change management of furnace bottom ash handling and its infrastructure, and add hydrogen production activity.

If Drax moves forward with the proposed bioenergy carbon capture and storage (BECC) project, CO2 captured at Drax Power Station would be transported via pipeline for permanent storage under the North Sea.

While Drax has been working to develop BECCS capacity for several years, the company in February 2026 announced it would deprioritize its investments in BECCS. “Given the current political environment and the lack of development of an appropriate regulatory framework to support the investment required for U.K. BECCS, the Group has refocused its investment priorities on nearer term opportunities with more balanced risk-return profiles and therefore has rationalized its level of investment in carbon capture opportunities,” Drax said in its 2025 financial report, released in February 2026. “Whilst U.K. BECCS is still an attractive option for the Group long term and management still believes that the development of BECCS at Drax Power Station is important to the U.K.'s Net Zero strategy, the full carrying amount of the development project of £47.6 million has been impaired due to the reduced likelihood of the project proceeding in the short to medium term. Although not expected in the near term, if an appropriate regulatory framework were to be developed and the political environment was to become more supportive of large-scale capital investment in U.K. BECCS, increasing the likelihood of the project progressing, a reversal of the impairment of certain U.K. BECCS costs may be required.”

Additional information, including a full copy of the U.K. Environment Agency’s decision document, is available on the U.K. government website.

text:
The European Commission on July 30 approved a EUR 290 million ($338.61 million) Dutch state aid package to support sustainable aviation fuel (SAF). The two approved support schemes aim to boost SAF supply and demand.

The two support schemes aim to support projects that produce SAF at different stages of their development. The schemes will share a common budget, but one will provide investment aid for SAF production while the other will help cover the costs of preparatory work for SAF projects, including front-end engineering design (FEED) studies.

Projects that use hydroprocessed esters and fatty acids (HEFA) technology will not be eligible for either scheme. Rather, the programs will exclusively support advanced non-HEFA SAF and synthetic aviation fuels (e-SAF).
